source_document.body:
Jaguar has unveiled the final version of its new Type 01 EV, the first car as part of its controversial rebrand, and it’s a 1,016 horsepower, four-door, 1930s-comic-book-mobster-style doozy.
Jaguar made waves in late 2024 when it revealed a new concept car (the Type 00) and a controversial rebranding, changing its wordmark and design language to be radically different from anything we’ve seen from the legendary marque before – or indeed, perhaps any automotive company.
Jaguar summarized the rebrand with the phrase “copy nothing,” and they seem to have hit that mark.
The redesign got a lot of attention, with much of it being negative, given what a departure it was for the brand. (Personally, I loved it, and perhaps loved it even more for each pearl that was clutched in response).
Advertisement - scroll for more content
A year later, the man responsible for the rebranding was fired from the company , leading some to think that the rebranding effort would be reversed and that something more traditional might come out of Jaguar.
And now, nearly another year later, we’re getting the first look at the first actual car to come out of the rebrand… and it looks very much like the Type 00 concept that attracted so much controversy, plus a couple doors and minus a little pink.
Jaguar has dubbed the car the Type 01 EV, which will be available in the 2028 model year. It’s the first production car to come out of the rebrand.
The styling is just as bold and unconventional as the concept, though Jaguar seems to have learned something from that experience and went with a little less unconventional coloring than the candy-cane pink that the Type 00 was originally clad in (again, I loved it, and your tears are delicious).
The hood is obnoxiously long – which is completely unnecessary, given the car’s electric provenance, and seems to exist primarily for styling reasons. Overall, the car is 204 inches (5.2 meters) long, half a foot longer than the Tesla Model S.
There’s a motor up there under the front hood (and two in the back), but there’s no way it takes up that much space, and Jaguars engineering graphics don’t suggest otherwise.
Jaguar says that the space between the front wheel and passenger compartment is meant to evoke the classic E-type , also known for its enormously long hood. To me, the straight lines, chopped top, and long, blocky hood all evoke the kind of vehicle I’d expect a comic book mobster to drive.
Those three motors combined put out 1,016 horsepower. They’ll get the 6,000lb beast from 0- to 60 in 3.1 seconds, and are attached to an 850-volt, 120kWh battery with 400 miles of EPA range. It can charge from 10-80% in 22 minutes on a 350kW DC charger, or add 200 miles of range in 13 minutes.
So we guess it would make a pretty good getaway car, too. Except, well, there’s no rear window to aim your tommy gun out of – instead, that’s solid, and you’ll have to see out the rear through a camera, like on the Polestar 4 coupe .
Inside, Jaguar has gone minimal, with few physical buttons anywhere to be seen and a central 7-inch interface that is styled similar to a smartphone. The center also has an armrest that runs down the length of the vehicle, with storage inside it, but which feels like it might lead the inside to feel a little cramped (and it does not obscure either a driveshaft or a battery, so it’s kind of just… there).
The car has its complement of luxurious features, like massage seats, cabin air purification and selectable fragrances.
Those luxury features are matched with a luxury price: starting at 130,000 British pounds ($172k). Which, while it’s over twice as expensive as Jaguar’s outgoing I-Pace EV, is maybe even somewhat cheap compared to the expectations for this vehicle, which ran upwards of $200k at one point.
As for the controversy, Jaguar seems to relish it. When Jaguar sent out surveys about its redesign, it got more 1s and 2s out of 10 than usual, but also more 9s and 10s. Jaguar’s managing director said “great design should have the confidence to polarize… we’re not interested in 6s, 7s, and 8s.”
Top comment by Simon
Liked by 1 people
I do like it, especially not in pink, but it says Jaguar about as much as my Frigidaire refrigerator.
Design language of these old fantastic sports car companies is their currency, they shouldn't throw that amazing artistic history in the waste basket as if its no longer relevant. Big mistake. Although it will be collectable for rich guys.
View all comments
If nothing else, we can commend them for not taking any half measures.
The car will be available to order in the start of 2027, but won’t deliver until later that year. So, if you’re looking to get in line, stay tuned.

Venture capital continued to flow into biopharma in the third quarter, though experts pointed out that investors remained selective, preferring to put their money behind advanced and derisked assets, as well as AI-driven drugmakers.
Venture capital funding into biopharma companies topped $16 billion in the first half of the year, and the money continued to flow into the industry in the third quarter. But it continues to be a story of haves and have nots, experts say.
“We’re seeing more capital being deployed even as overall deal activity remains constrained,” Dan Greaney, executive director of Life Sciences, Innovation Economy at J.P. Morgan, told BioSpace in an email interview. Money is “tending to flow toward later-stage, more de-risked assets, resulting in a small number of companies to receive larger amounts of capital.”
Proximal Ventures’ Sahir Raoof agreed. While biopharma is currently enjoying a “stronger financing environment,” the true picture is more nuanced. “The amount of money being raised doesn’t tell the story of how broadly that money is available,” he told BioSpace over email. “Capital is concentrated.”
Venture capital
5 largest VC rounds of H1 2026
Early-stage financing rounds are on track to hit their lowest dollar value in years as funders continue to eschew risky investments, experts told BioSpace .
July 8, 2026
·
9 min read
·
Tristan Manalac
Read more
Jim Polson, senior managing director at FTI Consulting, pointed to AdvanCell’s $315 million raise this quarter and Encoded’s $275 million as signs of “continued investor interest in more advanced, increasingly de-risked programs with clear paths to meaningful clinical milestones.” AdvanCell is pushing its lead radiopharma asset into Phase 3, while Encoded is also moving into pivotal development for its gene upregulation therapy for Dravet syndrome.
Another funding pattern that carried from the first half of the year to Q3 is the “growing investment in companies explicitly mentioning the use of AI and computational approaches to discover and develop medicines,” Raoof added.
He highlighted several of this year’s biggest rounds so far that have involved a focus on AI: Isomorphic Labs’ mammoth $2.1 billion series B , Parabilis Medicines’ $305 million series F and NewLimit’s $435 million series C . Raoof also pointed to Enveda, which uses a proprietary machine learning engine to unveil the therapeutic potential of molecules that already exist in nature. Enveda closed one of this quarter’s largest VC rounds.
Here, BioSpace takes a closer look at Enveda, AdvanCell and the other companies that raised Q3’s largest venture rounds.
Chai Discovery
Date: July 14
Round: Series C
Raise: $400 million
Topping the Q3 VC leaderboard is Chai Discovery, which in July commanded a $400 million round to further advance its AI models intended to accelerate preclinical drug discovery. The series C push, which included contributions from OpenAI and other big names, valued Chai at $3.8 billion.
Chai develops machine learning models that take into account biological structure and function to generate new molecules from scratch, the company said in the July news release. This approach aims to do away with the traditional trial-and-error approach to drug discovery and could open up disease targets that had previously been difficult to address.
Chai’s latest model is called Chai-3, which the biotech claims “materially improves” the success rates of generated antibodies over previous versions of the model.
This platform has won Chai many Big Pharma customers, including Eli Lilly, which in January brought the biotech on to create a purpose-built AI model exclusively for the pharma’s use. Financial details of the deal were not announced. Bristol Myers Squibb , Pfizer , Novartis and argenx have also lined up to work with Chai, each leveraging the biotech’s AI platform for de novo drug discovery.
Chai’s impressive fundraising round, led by Index Ventures, Kleiner Perkins, Sequioa Capital and Dimension, comes as tech money floods into biopharma , spurred by the rise of AI. The biggest symbol of this trend is Alphabet’s Isomorphic Labs, which in May raised $2.1 billion in series B money—the second-largest VC round in the industry’s history.
Artificial intelligence
With tech backing, AI biotechs force biopharma into ‘fail-fast’ drug development
AI is quickly becoming a central force in drug development, from powering pharma engines to permanently rewiring the capital markets.
August 12, 2026
·
6 min read
·
Tristan Manalac
Read more
AdvanCell
Date: July 16
Round: Series D
Raise: $315 million
Just days behind Chai is AdvanCell, which landed a $315 series D windfall that could help the Sydney- and Boston-based biotech break into one of the hottest modality markets in biopharma.
AdvanCell is developing targeted alpha radiotherapies for cancer. The company’s lead asset is ADVC001, a lead-212–based candidate designed to target the PSMA protein for the treatment of metastatic prostate cancer. ADVC001 is currently in a Phase 1b/2a study for this indication, with topline data expected in 2029. AdvanCell hopes to use the fundraising proceeds to advance the asset into late-stage development.
The series D will also allow the biotech to boost its U.S. manufacturing capabilities, supporting a better supply of the lead-212 isotope—largely in preparation for Phase 3 studies of the asset as well as future commercial demand. The new funding will also accelerate AdvanCell’s pipeline of targeted alpha candidates, the company said.
Ally Bridge Group and Alpha Wave co-led AdvanCell’s series D, with participation from big names across the industry, including Bain Capital Life Sciences, Eli Lilly and Sanofi Ventures.
Currently, the radiopharma space is dominated by Novartis , which owns the FDA-approved Lutathera, indicated for gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, and the prostate cancer therapy Pluvicto. Both of these products use the beta-emitter lutetium-177. The pharma is also developing a radiopharma therapy based on actinium-225, which belongs to the more powerful alpha-emitter class .
AdvanCell’s lead-212 isotope is also an alpha-emitting particle but has a much shorter half-life than actinium-225. This could enable a better safety profile, as is hinted at in the Phase 1b dose-escalation portion of AdvanCell’s Phase 1/2 TheraPb trial , which found no dose-limiting toxicities or treatment-related serious adverse events.
Radiopharmaceuticals
Radiopharma Powerhouses Push Frontiers With New Indications, Innovation
At the intersection of radiation and precision, Novartis, Bayer, AstraZeneca and more hope to cash in on a radiopharmaceuticals market that could top $16 billion by 2033.
May 12, 2025
·
9 min read
·
Tristan Manalac
Read more
Enveda
Date: Sept. 23
Round: Series E
Raise: $311 million
Hopping on the AI train is Enveda, which late last month collected $311 million in its series E round to advance a trio of drug candidates, including an “ exercise in a tablet ” asset for obesity. Enveda has now raised more than $845 million since its inception.
This investigational oral weight loss therapy, called ENV-308, showed “exceptional” gastrointestinal safety in a Phase 1 study that included 88 healthy adults, the company announced in August without providing specific data.
Enveda is also working on ENV-294, an oral drug candidate that in July lowered disease severity in a Phase 1 atopic dermatitis study. ENV-294 is also being tested for asthma . Then there’s ENV-6946, a TL1A+ pathway blocker being studied for inflammatory bowel disease.
Enveda plans to use the series E proceeds to advance its three clinical-stage assets into later-stage testing and explore their potential in other indications, the company said last month, noting that new trials are set to start in the coming months.
In addition, Enveda will use its fresh capital to continue developing its proprietary PRISM platform , an AI-powered engine that predicts the structures and therapeutic potential of existing molecules. Enveda currently has 14 development candidates, produced through PRISM, in preclinical development.
Enveda’s series E was led by Catalio Capital Management, with participation from T. Rowe Price Investment Management, Durable Capital Partners and Lightspeed.

AI drug hunter Enveda raises $311M for late-stage obesity, inflammatory disease push
Tech darling Enveda has raised a total of $845 million in the past six years. The latest funding round is intended to pave the way for an IPO someday.
September 23, 2026
·
1 min read
·
Annalee Armstrong
Read more
Encoded Therapeutics
Date: Sept. 9
Round: Series F
Raise: $275 million
Precision medicine developer Encoded Therapeutics makes the cut for this list with its $275 million series F round early last month, which the company plans to use to take its lead asset into pivotal development.
Encoded is working on ETX101, an investigational gene upregulation therapy that the biotech is positioning as a one-time therapy for Dravet syndrome, a rare epileptic encephalopathy caused by mutations in the SCN1A gene. ETX101, which is delivered directly into the brain, boosts the expression of SCN1A .
The asset is in the Phase 1/2 POLARIS study, which last month showed a strong reduction in monthly countable seizures. The series F money will help drive pivotal development for ETX101. Encoded also plans to use the proceeds to build up another asset, dubbed ETX391, for a 2027 regulatory filing seeking permission to start clinical testing.
Aside from advancing its pipeline, part of the series F haul will also go toward scaling up manufacturing capabilities, Encoded said.
Encoded’s fundraising push was co-led by GV (Google Ventures) and an undisclosed healthcare fund. Other institutional investors to participate included Illumina Ventures, RTW Investments and ARCH Venture Partners.
Funding
Encoded raises $275M series F for Dravet syndrome gene therapy
Encoded Therapeutics’ lead asset ETX101 is a gene therapy being tested for Dravet syndrome. Phase 1/2 data showed substantial reductions in seizures.
September 10, 2026
·
2 min read
·
Tristan Manalac
Read more
Solstice Oncology
Date: Sept. 9
Round: Series A
Raise: $225 million
Capping off this list is Solstice Oncology, which had the biggest biopharma launch in Q3, netting $225 million for its series A round in early September.
Solstice will use the money to bankroll the development of porustobart, an anti-CTLA-4 antibody that the startup licensed from China’s Harbour BioMed for $105 million, covering a $50 million upfront payment, $5 million in near-term commitments and $50 million in Solstice equity. The Boston-based biotech also put up to $1.1 billion on the line in development, regulatory and commercial milestones.
Solstice plans to combine porustobart with Merck’s mega-blockbuster PD-1 drug Keytruda. The FDA has given the go-ahead for the regimen to be tested in a Phase 2 study for neoadjuvant advanced colon cancer and another undisclosed disease, with data slated for the back half of 2027.
A Phase 2 study conducted by Harbour showed that porustobart, when used alongside BeOne Medicines’ PD-1 inhibitor Tevimbra, elicited a 30% objective response rate as a late-line option in patients with microsatellite-stable metastatic colorectal cancer without liver metastases, Solstice said in September .
Solstice’s series A was led by RA Capital Management, with participation from Forbion, Canaan Partners and other backers.
Venture capital
Solstice rises with $225M to develop next-gen CTLA-4 drug from China
Solstice Oncology, founded in February, is emerging from stealth having already secured an investigational new drug application from the FDA for a Phase 2 trial of a CTLA-4 antibody purchased from China’s Harbour BioMed.

source_document.body:
The person you expect to address the company’s problems should know the challenges your business faces. Not having that context will limit what they can accomplish.
There is a point in many executive searches when stewarding the candidate begins to take precedence over informing the candidate. The science is presented at its most promising. The financial outlook is delivered with an optimistic reading. Problems within the leadership team are softened. Disagreement in the boardroom is framed as “healthy debate.” A difficult history attached to the role gets abbreviated because everyone is focused on the future.
This is not the approach I would advise. I have spent over five decades placing key leaders in life sciences, and I have never believed that difficult information makes an opportunity less compelling. It makes the mandate honest. The person you expect to address the company’s problems should know what those challenges are before agreeing to take responsibility for them.
A search is not a sales process
There is nothing wrong with enthusiasm. I become concerned when enthusiasm starts replacing disclosure.
Senior executives are not being recruited into abstractions. They are inheriting companies with histories. Directors are stepping into boards with histories of their own. Decisions have already been made, programs have succeeded or disappointed and investors have expectations. Perhaps the board and management do not agree as completely as everyone would like a candidate to believe. That context affects what an incoming leader can accomplish.
Suppose you hire an executive to repair a function, but minimize how serious the problems within that function have become. The executive may be perfectly capable of fixing it. But you have sent that person into the company with a faulty diagnosis. Now some portion of the first months is spent discovering what was already known. That is an unnecessary handicap to impose on someone you presumably went to considerable trouble and expense to hire.
It also creates an immediate question of trust. Once an executive or director discovers that material information was sanitized during recruitment, he or she is entitled to—and likely will—wonder what else received the same treatment.
Bad news may help you make the right hire
I understand why companies and boards hesitate to be transparent. They have found an exceptional candidate and do not want to lose that person over an ugly problem. But what have you gained if the truth would cause the candidate to decline? An executive search is not successful because somebody signs an employment agreement or accepts a board seat. The appointment has to work.
An experienced leader may even be more interested after hearing the difficult parts. Strong executives and directors tend to know that formidable jobs come with formidable problems. They deserve a clear picture of the obstacles ahead and confidence that the company or board, as appropriate, will give them the authority and support to address them.
A clear picture is especially important in life sciences. I have seen teams become enamored with what someone accomplished elsewhere. Those accomplishments matter, but they do not tell you how that individual will respond to the new circumstances at hand.
That is why candor during the search matters so much. You cannot learn how a candidate will approach a difficult financing environment, a program that has disappointed, tension within the leadership team or board or expectations that need to be reset if you have tidied up those realities before presenting the opportunity. You are evaluating the candidate against one version of the assignment while asking that person to accept another.
A serious search should give both sides enough information to have a harder conversation. Consider: “Here is where we are. Here is what needs attention. Tell us how you would approach it.” That discussion tells me far more about a prospective leader than another hour spent reviewing what he or she accomplished somewhere else.
Tell candidates what they are actually being hired to solve
Before going to market, company leadership and, where appropriate, the board should be able to speak plainly about the mandate. Where is the company falling short? What has already been attempted? What does the next person need to address that has not been addressed successfully before? The answers will not all belong in a job specification or director profile. They do belong somewhere in a serious search process.
There are obvious boundaries. Confidentiality matters, and candidates are not entitled to privileged information. That said, maintaining confidentiality should not cross the line into projecting an image of the leadership or organization that feels entirely foreign to insiders. Search firms need to resist that temptation, too.
A search partner who thinks the job is to keep the candidate excited has misunderstood the assignment. We should test whether the opportunity and the individual genuinely match, which is impossible when one side works from incomplete information.
What happens after the search matters
Getting a candidate to say yes is not the objective. Placing the right person in the position with a fair opportunity to succeed is.
I began my career as a scientist, and perhaps that is why I have always wanted to start with the facts, including the ones we may not particularly like. You cannot expect an executive to make strategic decisions from incomplete information. You cannot expect a director to contribute at the level you recruited that person for if important realities only become clear after the appointment.
And in life sciences, we do not have the luxury of pretending that lost time is inconsequential. Companies have clinical and regulatory work to advance. They have capital to manage. There are people inside these organizations who need pragmatic leadership, and there are real patients waiting for the work to produce something meaningful.
This is why I have very little patience for dressing up an opportunity during a search. Tell candidates what is good about it. Tell them what is not working. If something is ugly, they need to understand that, too. Then listen carefully to what they would do about it.
Their response may tell you more about their ability to lead or govern than all the selling in the world.
